prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of time-reversal-invariant topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect, and for its experimental discovery in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: B018 is the cleanest example on the shortlist of what the prize is meant to reward: a discovery with an identifiable origin and an identifiable experimental confirmation. Kane and Mele supplied the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall proposal, and Molenkamp's group observed helical edge transport in HgTe/CdTe quantum wells. The result has been confirmed in several material systems and by independent techniques over roughly two decades, so the interpretation is stable and recognition is not premature. Eight members ranked it, which is the broadest support on the shortlist, and five of them put it in their top three or first place. As a materials physicist I also value that the concept turned into a practical search for real materials, and that it rests on well-characterised interfaces and edges, where the experimental evidence can be checked directly.
statement.case_against: The three-name configuration is an incomplete account of the history. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe quantum-well proposal that guided Molenkamp's experiment, and the three-dimensional topological insulator work (Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Hasan and others) is a neighbouring contribution that a citation framed too broadly would have to either include or exclude. Zhang is deceased, which complicates any reconstruction. The 2016 prize on topological phase transitions and phases may also be read as having partly honoured the area. A citation that is written narrowly around the quantum spin Hall state is therefore important, and it will still leave some real contributors unrecognised.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B018 first, calling it a prediction promptly realised in nature, and notes that Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and the 3D topological insulator discoverers sit near the boundary of the configuration.
responses.response: I agree with the scientific assessment and with the boundary concern. I would resolve it by keeping the citation tied to the 2D quantum spin Hall state and its first observation, not to topological insulators in general. The HgTe proposal is then a closely related contribution that we acknowledge, not one we try to repair by adding names. I would not widen to the 3D work, because Fu-Kane-Mele and the ARPES observations are a second discovery with its own attribution questions, and a three-person limit cannot hold both fairly.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first because it is a two-name, cleanly attributed invention that is mature, reproduced by many national laboratories and distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
responses.response: I take the attribution argument seriously: B041 has the tidier credit, and I moved it only to fourth in my opening ballot because it lies outside my own field, not because I doubt it. My reservation is not novelty relative to earlier prizes. It is that B018 offers both the originating theory and the decisive experiment in a single finding, with a longer record of independent confirmation across material classes. I would keep B041 as my second alternative, and I would not object to it as the prize if the committee decides that a precision-measurement invention should take priority this year.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks twisted bilayer graphene first for a simple continuum model that organises a large range of phenomena, with a clean theory-plus-experiment attribution, and sees B018 as arguably overdue but exposed to the 2016 overlap.
responses.response: I agree that the attribution of B030 is clean, since Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat bands and Jarillo-Herrero's group observed the correlated states. My difficulty is maturity. The mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, and twist-angle disorder and sample dependence raise questions about reproducibility that I know from imaging work on layered materials. I would prefer to wait several years. On the 2016 overlap, Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz were recognised for topological phase transitions and the quantum Hall-type phases, not for time-reversal-invariant topological insulators, so I read this as a distinct discovery.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit quantum electrodynamics first and ranks B018 only sixth, accepting the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp allocation as reasonable but incomplete, while acknowledging that the cap on laureates forces an unresolved choice for his own candidate.
responses.response: I appreciate the disclosure of his own proximity to that field. I share the worry about the three-person cap in B020, where Girvin's exclusion is a real problem, and the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits makes the timing delicate. For B018 I would say that an incomplete allocation is not by itself disqualifying, since three credited names do represent the decisive theory and the decisive experiment. If the committee regards the omission of Bernevig and Hughes as serious, I would want that argument made on the history, not as a general penalty for the candidate.

uncertainties: How the committee should treat the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal, which guided the experiment but is outside the supplied credited names and cannot include Zhang.
Whether the 2016 prize is judged to have partly honoured topological phases, which would weigh against B018.
My opening placed B041 fourth and B030 third, and I have not fully tested either against a recent-prize overlap argument. Metrology is outside my own field.
I rely on my own recollection of the priority history, and have not verified it independently.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B018: Kane, Mele and Molenkamp are not among my documented connections. My documented ties are to Chalmers colleagues, early work with David R. Clarke at IBM, academic exchanges in Japan (relevant only in a general sense to Katori of B041) and the international microscopy federation. Göran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague and the lead proponent of B020, so I would not treat my views on that candidate as independent of the committee's own conflict check.
